[07:54] Enter into section 2 on page 3.

[08:07] You will hear an audio guide introducing visitors to a museum.

[08:12] First you have some time to look at questions 11-15 on page 3, and answer questions 11-15.

[08:55] Welcome to the Global Museum, located at the heart of this truly multicultural city, which is home to more than 60 different nationalities.

[09:05] The museum has a number of exciting displays and exhibitions, and this audio guide is designed to help you make the most of your visit.

[09:13] Altogether, the museum has 18 different galleries, and this season sees the opening of three

[09:19] new exhibitions. We recommend that you begin your tour by visiting this season's highlights.

[09:26] The Heritage Clothes exhibition is located in Gallery 5 of the museum. People who live

[09:32] in the area have spent two years preparing this exhibition, which brings together some

[09:37] of the fascinating garments traditionally worn in their own communities. They research

[09:43] the history of their community's clothing traditions and the customs and rituals associated

[09:48] with them. All together, 16 countries are represented, from Ghana to Korea, from Turkey

[09:55] to Nepal. The photographs that accompany each display case were taken by some of the city

[10:01] college students who were studying design and show the clothes being modelled by the

[10:06] real people who wear them in the course of their everyday lives.

[10:11] Another highlight this season is the exhibition called Toys from the Past, which can be found

[10:16] in Gallery 9. This exhibition, which will appeal to people of all ages, is on tour

[10:22] throughout the country and will be here for 10 weeks only. The exhibits include dolls made

[10:28] over 100 years ago with beautiful porcelain faces and, in some cases, real hair.

[10:35] The collection covers the favourite toys such as wooden trainsets from many different

[10:40] generations and provides plenty of interest for children and adults.

[10:46] The gigantic board games, which are laid out on the gallery floor, are one of the most

[10:50] popular activities in the exhibition and should not be missed.

[10:55] This exhibition concludes with a special display of miniature toys.

[10:59] These small objects are on loan from countries all over the world, and in some cases measure no more than a few centimeters.

[11:08] There's a tiny car made from matchsticks, a toy airplane complete with pilots and passengers made out of seashells,

[11:15] and some exquisite little buildings no higher than four centimeters.

[11:19] Here the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20 on pages 3 and 4, and answer questions 16 to 20.

[12:07] The final gallery highlight of the season is the Biscuit Gallery, number 15.

[12:13] Many years ago, this city was famous for its biscuits, although today the factory no longer exists.

[12:20] Did you know, for example, that before biscuits were packed in paper or cardboard boxes,

[12:25] Biscuit tins were fashion items. The factory made tins round, square, triangular, hexagonal

[12:33] for a whole range of different occasions to celebrate national events, festivals, famous

[12:40] faces and so on. One fascinating display deals with people's favourite biscuits. There

[12:47] are sweet biscuits and savoury ones. Biscuits filled with jam and biscuits filled with currants.

[12:52] Biscuits with pink, yellow and white sugar icing or coloured sugar flowers.

[12:59] When the factory finally closed, it announced that people's favourite biscuit was not as

[13:04] you might expect a chocolate biscuit or one filled with jam and cream, but a plain savoury

[13:10] one which was eaten with cheese.

[13:14] When you get to the end of the exhibition, there's an entertaining hands-on activity

[13:19] to fill your own biscuit tin.

[13:21] All the biscuits ever produced by the company are piled up on a table along with various tins.

[13:28] The biscuits are made out of thin pieces of wood, but the weight, colours and shapes replicate the original biscuits.

[13:36] Your job is to fill a tin with biscuits so that when the lid is taken off, they sit there as neatly as they did when the job was done by machine.

[13:44] It's not as easy as it looks.

[13:47] If you would like to buy a memento of your visit, there is a museum gift shop selling

[13:51] postcards, souvenirs, and handmade pottery next to the information desk on the ground

[13:57] floor.

[13:59] And finally, if you don't want to carry your coats and bags around with you during your

[14:02] visit, please make use of the free lockers provided by the museum.

[14:07] Enjoy your visit.

[21:42] Turn to section 4 on page 7. You will hear part of a talk about research into learner persistence given by a university lecturer to her colleagues.

[22:05] First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on pages 7 and 8.

[22:52] Listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

[23:00] About a research study I did over a period of 5 years on learner persistence.

[23:06] Why some people stick at academic study better than others.

[23:11] As teachers, you will know that there is a tremendous variation in the learner's response to certain things.

[23:17] For example, a short period of illness might completely destabilize some students and cause them to give up their degree studies.

[23:27] Other learners might overcome tremendous difficulties to stay the course.

[23:32] I am particularly interested in this second group, who are the ones with learner persistence.

[23:38] What I decided to do was design a research study using a sample of my university's third-year undergraduate students,

[23:48] 295 in all, who obviously had already stayed the course pretty well.

[23:54] The sample was drawn from a range of ages, but there was deliberately a significant number of mature students,

[24:02] and all respondents were living at home in the local region.

[24:05] I wanted to have this element of consistency, not having some coming from outside the area

[24:12] and living in university accommodation.

[24:15] It should be noted though that there was significant variation in home background to reflect the

[24:21] variation in our student population.

[24:24] I designed questionnaires which were devised to elicit what their concerns had been as

[24:29] they started the course and what had sustained them throughout the three years.

[24:34] Findings from the first section indicated that their worries when they started varied from financial concerns, though this had not been as strong as I expected, to career prospects.

[24:47] But mature students with children tended to emphasize uncertainties about their relationship with them.

[24:54] The second section of my questionnaire looked at learner persistence under three main headings

[25:04] social and environmental factors, other factors, and intrinsic or personal characteristics.

[25:13] I identified three levels of importance for each of these.

[25:16] At the first level, those points identified by participants as most important in learner

[25:22] persistence.

[25:23] For social factors, many respondents said how crucial it had been to have good support,

[25:30] though there was no one specific source. It could be family or friends.

[25:35] As regards other factors, students are heartened not so much by high grades,

[25:41] but by what they regard as success in study.

[25:45] And for personal characteristics, many respondents reported that they took pleasure in challenge,

[25:51] and that this was regarded as very significant.

[25:55] At the second level of importance, in the first category,

[25:59] a sizable percentage talked about the fact that they had enjoyed themselves

[26:03] in school as an important social factor.

[26:07] In the second column, Other Factors, a number of people said that

[26:11] what was of most importance was decent health.

[26:14] This had a fairly strong influence on their persistence in their studies.

[26:18] And then, under the heading of personal characteristics, there were quite a large percentage of respondents

[26:25] who mentioned they felt it was important to have lots of interests in their everyday lives.

[26:32] This gave them a depth and sense of perspective which less persistent learners might lack.

[26:38] And then, onto the third level.

[26:41] Under social factors, several respondents talked about good relationships with their tutors.

[26:46] For other factors, they mentioned lack or absence of any problems in their families.

[26:53] And finally, under column 3, they identified an ability to juggle several roles,

[26:58] what we might call their capacity for multitasking.

[27:02] Now, these findings obviously helped inform the design of activities, as I mentioned.

[27:08] But in addition, a number of further recommendations emerged.

[27:12] First, I propose that the department distributes questionnaires to first-year students to help

[27:18] get an idea of their maturity when starting the course.

[27:22] This is really our overriding concern.

[27:26] Secondly, I recommend we look into ways of offering induction courses for some selected

[27:31] students to allow them to take on the role of advisors.

[27:36] We think they are the best people to act in that role.

[27:38] This policy will make support much more accessible to our students.

[27:45] Thirdly, this help is often most needed in the evening and night when offices are closed

[27:50] and so we should set up online services instead of the more traditional telephone services.

[27:57] Research has shown that these services are actually more accessible to the majority of students.

[28:03] And finally, it is often important to be proactive.

[28:07] If students are not meeting deadlines, then someone should contact them rather than wait for them to come to us.

[28:16] Now, are there any questions about the points?

[28:21] That is the end of Section 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
